rationale: A wins because it knows where the facts stop. It correctly refuses "Dating apps are all turning to AI to stop the subscriber bleed" as a hallucinated category trend, while B keeps "Dating apps are selling AI to users who say AI ruins dating," turning one Bumble relaunch and "some users" into a market story it has not earned. B is sharper in places, but that kept trend angle is the kind of confident overreach a reporter checks once and bins.
gaps_in_A: "The relaunch is live now and it is the first product the returned founder has put their name on since coming back this year" overstates the update; the facts say the relaunch is under the returning founder-CEO, not that it is the first product she has put her name on.
"Bumble sells subscriptions" is a reasonable inference from paying users, but it is still an inference; a markets angle should pin that to filings before pitching.

"What happens when Bumble's AI writes your opening line" is useful but overlaps with the women-message-first tension; it needs sharper separation as a hands-on service piece, not another authenticity debate.
The product-review angle depends on reporter access and real interactions; without that, it collapses into launch-description filler.
gaps_in_B: "Dating apps are selling AI to users who say AI ruins dating" is the major foul: the update gives Bumble plus some user criticism, not a plural category trend or the stronger claim that users say AI "ruins" dating.
"Bumble is a usable anchor rather than the whole story" admits the trend angle needs evidence B does not have, then keeps it anyway. That is how bad trend pitches are born.
"the first substantive product move since the founder's return this year" is not in the supplied facts; maybe true, maybe not, but it cannot be asserted from this update.

The suggested next step, "newsjack-detector," is less directly useful than resolving reporters for the strongest angle; this set already has a current company update, not a missing-news-discovery problem.
